new_statements.quote: In disyllabic words, the primary stress always occurs on the last syllable together with either a secondary stress or no stress occurring on the other syllable of the word. [p. 34:] Primary stress, which functions as the nucleus syllable of the word, always occurs on a monosyllabic word and on the final syllable of a disyllabic word. Secondary stress or unstress, occurs on the syllable preceding the final syllable of the word. The phonological word structures are predictable according to the rule stated above, therefore, it is non-phonemic. It is not necessary to write any stress mark on words in phonemic writing.
new_statements.citation: Pornsawan Ploykaew. 2001. Samre Grammar. Ph.D. (Linguistics) thesis, Institute of Language and Culture for Rural Development, Mahidol University, Nakhon Pathom. xx+350 leaves. ISBN 9746656287.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (371 pp., the PDF's metadata gives the Title 'Samre Grammar', Author Pornsawan Ploykaew; title page PDF p. 1 = 'SAMRE GRAMMAR.. Doctor of Philosophy (Linguistics), Mahidol University, 2001, ISBN 974-665-628-7'). Rendered PDF pp. 54-55 (printed pp. 33-34) as images and read them myself. Both quoted sentences are on the page verbatim: p. 33 sec. 2.3.3.2 'In disyllabic words, the primary stress always occurs on the last syllable together with either a secondary stress or no stress occurring on the other syllable of the word.'; p. 34 sec. 2.3.4 'Primary stress, which functions as the nucleus syllable of the word, always occurs on a monosyllabic word and on the final syllable of a disylla…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per phonological word ('stress group'), always on the last syllable: the sole syllable of a monosyllable, the final (major) syllable of a disyllable, and the final syllable of the rare trisyllables (native /sammaweek/, /siilaman/ and Thai loans, all [ˇS.ˇS.'S]). Stress is fully predictable and non-phonemic. Word boundaries are located from stress: 'The primary stress always falls on the last syllable, so the word break will follow the primary stress syllable' (p. 35).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Three degrees: primary, secondary, unstressed (p. 32). In disyllables the non-final syllable takes either secondary stress (sub-type A, [ˇS.'S], e.g. /saliəŋ/ [ˇsa.'liəŋ] 'woman') or no stress (sub-type B, [S.'S], reduced/syllabic-nasal presyllables, e.g. /m̩luəŋ/ [m̩.'luəŋ] 'man'); in trisyllables both non-final syllables take secondary stress. Unstressed nasal presyllables have neutral pitch with no tone contrast (p. 66); tones function in syllables with primary or secondary stress (p. 65).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; Thai loanword trisyllables also carry final primary stress. Presyllables may collapse (deleted, reduced to syllabic nasal), which changes the number of syllables but not the final-stress rule (pp. 42-43).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (= stress group), described as the unit between the intonation group and the syllable; citation-form and in-sentence examples both given. Sentence-level emphasis stress exists separately ('a main sentence stress which can be shifted around', ch. 6, PDF p. 204). Language is tonal (three tones A/B/C on stressed syllables), so stress and tone coexist; stress is non-phonemic, tone is phonemic.
new_statements.identity_note: All three Ploykaew sources describe Samre as spoken at Ban Mamuang, Tambon Nonsi, Bo Rai District, Trat Province, Thailand (ISO 639-3 sxm; 20-30 speakers in 1998-2001), not the extinct Samre of Siem Reap, Cambodia. Glottolog 5.3 has retired samr1245 'Samre of Siem Reap' to bookkeeping and merged it into somr1240 'Somray of Battambang-Somre of Siem Reap' [smu]; Glottolog nevertheless links Ploykaew's works to sxm/samr1245, and ISO sxm as used by Ethnologue is the Thai (Trat) Samre. The Siem Reap variety itself is attested only by 19th-century wordlists (Moura 1883, compiled in Headley 1977) with no stress description. The statement applies to Thai Samre (Western Pearic, close to Chong/Kasong).

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement (final primary stress, predictable, non-phonemic) as the existing statement, which comes from this very thesis; this listed '1986 MA thesis' is not a separate document. The Glottolog record 148832 is bibliographic only (no file; sealang.net/sala/archives/pdf8/ returns 404) and its SALA key reads pornsawan2001samre; the 2001 MKS 31 article lists 'Samre grammar' as the Ph.D. dissertation in progress; the 2001 thesis bibliography self-cites only Ploykaew 1999 and its biography records an MA at Mahidol 1983-85 with no title. No evidence of a 1986 Samre grammar exists; the record is best treated as a misdated duplicate of the 2001 Ph.D. thesis, which was read.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every phonological word (stress group) has exactly one primary stress, on its only syllable if monosyllabic and on the last syllable if di- or trisyllabic; the non-final syllable(s) are presyllables carrying secondary stress or no stress. Stress is fully predictable and therefore non-phonemic (not written). Samre also has three tones (A, B, C) on the stressed major syllable; the pitch of an unstressed nasal presyllable is neutral and non-contrastive (pp. 65-66).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Non-final syllables take either secondary stress (sub-type A, [ˇS.ˈS], e.g. /saliəŋ/ [ˇsa.ˈliəŋ] 'woman') or no stress (sub-type B, [S.ˈS], presyllable reduced to a syllabic nasal, e.g. /m̩luəŋ/ [m̩.ˈluəŋ] 'man'); the two native trisyllables and Thai loans are [ˇS.ˇS.ˈS] with secondary stress on both non-final syllables (p. 34). Sec. 2.4.4.2 (p. 42): the presyllable 'will take the weak stress or unstressed and will always occupy the initial position of the word'; presyllables frequently collapse or are deleted.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; trisyllabic words are rare (two native forms plus Thai loans) and also carry final primary stress. Stress is called non-phonemic; the primary stress also serves as the word-boundary cue: 'The primary stress always falls on the last syllable, so the word break will follow the primary stress syllable' (p. 35).
new_statements.identity_note: Ploykaew describes the Samre of Thailand, recorded at Ban Ma-muang and Ban Nonsi, Bo-rai District, Trat Province (fieldwork Oct 1998 - Mar 1999, rechecked Mar 2000), not the Samre of Siem Reap, Cambodia known only from Moura's 1883 wordlist. Glottolog's samr1245 is a retired bookkeeping entry assigned to ISO sxm by computerized assignment from the word 'samre'; Glottolog now groups the Cambodian variety with Somray of Battambang [smu]. The stress statement therefore belongs to Thai Samre (ISO sxm as used by Ethnologue), and the record's '1986 MA thesis' date is unsupported (see relation_note).
